components.gap: Retain, for the empirical claim that base-rate-neglect responses are relevance values given in place of the requested posterior probability or odds, Merin's own statement of the base-rate-neglect case (p. 273): the prior odds for H are tacitly set to one and so fail to reflect information supplied on the experimenter's instruction sheet that should warrant a skewed prior, for example P(H) >> P(not H), before observation E impinges; with that neglect the posterior odds equal the likelihood-ratio value of relevance. The handbook gives only the arithmetic (handbook/parts/p15/rationality-4-3.tex lines 479-483: replacing prior odds by one makes posterior odds equal L) and states instead that Merin reports no task or design for this phenomenon (handbook/parts/p15/inductive-logic-and-confirmation-w02b-p15-024.tex lines 878-883). Every measure definition, completion clause and worked contrast with posterior probability is otherwise present.

Reconstruct the source's remaining definitional and argumentative steps, each absent from the handbook: (a) Merin's reasons for taking Definition 3 (the covariance form) as the definition of qualitative relevance: it depends on Definition 2 for its intuition but needs no completion clause and reveals the symmetry of the relevance relations (p. 266); (b) his remark that, because P(A) = P(A | T) for any tautology T, Definition 3 is the special case of conditional irrelevance, Definition 5, on a tautological condition (p. 267); (c) his statement that Carnap's covariance measure R_C is amount-symmetric although it violates POP-D (p. 272): the handbook gives only the POP-D half (rationality-4-3.tex lines 449-451; w02b-p15-024 Theorem z-characterization item 3); (d) his remark that the ordinal classes yielded by Theorem 7 determine the specific measures D, Q, L, QL, LL, KO and Z only under further conditions, among them smoothness (p. 271): rationality-4-3.tex lines 341-342 say the classes do not single out a transform but do not name the further conditions; (e) the premise of his base-rate-neglect argument, namely Merin's own statement of the base-rate-neglect case (p. 273): the prior odds for H are tacitly set to one and so fail to reflect information supplied on the experimenter's instruction sheet that should warrant a skewed prior, for example P(H) >> P(not H), before observation E impinges; with that neglect the posterior odds equal the likelihood-ratio value of relevance.

(a) Present the base-rate-neglect example under its stated assumptions, namely Merin's own statement of the base-rate-neglect case (p. 273): the prior odds for H are tacitly set to one and so fail to reflect information supplied on the experimenter's instruction sheet that should warrant a skewed prior, for example P(H) >> P(not H), before observation E impinges; with that neglect the posterior odds equal the likelihood-ratio value of relevance, and classify its empirical content as the source gives it: handbook/parts/p15/inductive-logic-and-confirmation-w02b-p15-024.tex lines 878-883 say that Merin reports no task, population, design, measure or uncertainty for either base-rate neglect or the conjunction fallacy, whereas p. 273 states the requested quantity (posterior probability or odds), the neglected instruction-sheet information and, for Linda, the ranking task and the representativeness design, which handbook/parts/p15/inductive-logic-and-confirmation-w02c-p15-027.tex lines 595-625 itself records. (b) The inventory of the chapter's claims by kind, which promises every claim of the chapter (inductive-logic-and-confirmation-w02c-p15-027.tex lines 29-30 and 698-920), omits the summary's two self-descriptions (that the abstract theory of qualitative relevance is explored quite fully, notably the role of conditional irrelevance, and that the central role of relevance for reasoning is emphasized throughout, p. 265) and the intuitive qualification attached to Theorem 1 (if A speaks for B, then B speaks for A, however weakly (intuitively), p. 266).
